payload.unusable_reason: Constitution Bench answered a reference on points of law only (future prospects, deduction, multiplier, conventional heads); it awarded no amount and sent the matters back to the appropriate Bench.

precedent.holding: Future prospects for deceased up to 60: permanent job 50% (under 40), 30% (40-50), 15% (50-60); self-employed or fixed pay 40%, 25%, 10%; none above 60; income after tax. Deduction and multiplier per 2009 standards, multiplier by deceased's age. Loss of estate Rs 15,000, consortium Rs 40,000, funeral Rs 15,000, up 10% every three years; no separate children's-care head.

extraction.title_anon: Five-judge Supreme Court ruling on how death compensation is worked out (law only, no award)
extraction.family_summary: On 31 October 2017 a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court settled how tribunals across India must work out compensation when someone dies in a road accident. It awarded no money to any family; the appeals went back to other benches to be decided under these rules. The income of the person who died is raised to allow for future pay rises: by 50%, 30% or 15% (under 40, 40 to 50, 50 to 60) for a permanent job, and by 40%, 25% or 10% for the self-employed or people on fixed pay; nothing is added over 60. It fixed Rs 15,000 for loss of estate, Rs 40,000 for loss of a spouse's company (consortium) and Rs 15,000 for the funeral, each rising 10% every three years.
what_mattered: Earlier Supreme Court rulings disagreed on whether the self-employed get a future-prospects addition; the five-judge bench said they do, at a lower rate than permanent employees.
For people in permanent jobs aged 50 to 60, the court added 15% for future pay rises where earlier rulings had allowed nothing; the self-employed and those on fixed pay in that age group get 10%.

Fixed sums for loss of estate (Rs 15,000), loss of a spouse's company (Rs 40,000) and funeral (Rs 15,000) replaced varying amounts, such as Rs 1 lakh for consortium in a 2013 ruling, and rise 10% every three years; there is no separate amount for children's loss of care and guidance.
The share deducted for the deceased's own living costs, and the multiplier, which goes by the deceased's age, stay as set in a 2009 Supreme Court ruling.
